lesson.title: RIP: Distance Vector Routing You Can Actually Run
lesson.summary: RIP, the Routing Information Protocol, is one of the earliest and simplest real world implementations of distance vector routing, using hop count as its metric and capping distances at 15 hops.
lesson.body:
Distance vector routing is an algorithm, RIP, the Routing Information Protocol, is one of the oldest concrete protocols that actually runs it on real routers. RIP was formally documented as an early Internet standard, first in RFC 1058 in 1988, with an updated version, RIPv2, in RFC 2453 a decade later. Like any RFC document, these specifications spell out precisely how the protocol's messages are formatted and how routers using it must behave, so that equipment from different vendors can all speak RIP correctly to each other.

RIP's defining choice is its metric: instead of measuring cost in terms of bandwidth, delay, or any administrator assigned weight, it simply counts hops, the number of routers a packet must pass through to reach its destination. Every link, in RIP's eyes, costs exactly 1. That simplicity is deliberate, RIP was built for small, relatively uniform networks, where counting hops is close enough to counting cost, and where the complexity of a richer metric was not worth the trouble.

To bound how large that hop count can get, RIP defines 15 as the maximum usable distance and 16 as infinity, meaning unreachable. Any destination whose best known hop count reaches 16 is treated as unreachable and effectively removed from use. This ceiling is not arbitrary busywork, it is RIP's safety valve for the count to infinity problem covered in the next chapter, a scenario where distance vector's own update rule can cause routers to keep raising a stale distance estimate for a failed route. Because RIP caps distances at 16, that runaway counting is guaranteed to stop quickly rather than climb forever, at the cost of RIP being unusable on any network where a legitimate path might need more than 15 hops.

In practice, RIP routers exchange their full distance vectors with directly connected neighbors roughly every 30 seconds, and each router applies the same core update rule from the distance vector chapter: for every destination a neighbor advertises, check whether the cost to that neighbor plus the neighbor's advertised hop count beats what is already in the table, and if so, adopt it. RIP is rarely the protocol of choice in large modern networks, since its hop count metric ignores bandwidth and its 15 hop ceiling is far too small for the modern internet's scale, but its simplicity is exactly what makes it a good first protocol to study: nearly everything it does is distance vector routing in its most direct, unadorned form.
